intro.en: Rev 1 — narration from the recording, cleaned ("aerof foil / aerofall / air foil" → aerofoil, "cord" → chord, "swelling vortex" → swirling vortex, "on route" → en-route, "yor and sid slip" → yaw and sideslip, "rootto tip" → root-to-tip, "climax / clax" → CLmax, "edge of store" → edge of the stall, "route" → root, "platform" → planform, "installed behavior" → stall behaviour, "weight turbulence / the weight dissipates" → wake turbulence / the wake dissipates, "in force" → enforce, "prime" → climb, "C underscore D = K C_L 2" → CDi = k·CL², "FRA 1 pi E A R" → 1 ÷ (π·e·AR), "OS efficiency factor" → Oswald efficiency factor, "YC underscore L squared" → why CL squared, "rake tips" → raked tips, "MAC" → Mach, "crews" → cruise, "frack" → fraction, "CDM" → CDmin, "tail plane incident" → tailplane incidence). Before teaching: (1) page 6 and the recording have spanwise flow BACKWARDS. On the upper surface the flow drifts from tip toward root (inward); on the lower surface it flows from root toward tip (outward), because the pressure difference leaks away at the tip. Where the two sheets meet at the trailing edge they form the vortex sheet that rolls up into the tip vortices (the air goes out under the wing, up round the tip and in over the top; seen from behind, the right-tip vortex turns anticlockwise and the left-tip vortex clockwise); (2) page 5 says the horizontal stabiliser "experiences upwash from the main wing" — wrong; the tailplane sits in the wing's downwash (the recording says this correctly); page 5 also has garbled text ("Similar laner flow pressents…"); (3) page 3 defines AoA against the "longitudinal axis (or chord line in 2D)" — AoA is measured from the chord line (the recording is correct); (4) page 1 cover shows "081 01 03 00 Coefficients" — wrong code/title for this deck; (5) page 12 shows induced drag as the "major contributor" in typical cruise and "a significant part of total drag at cruising speeds" — in cruise parasite drag is the larger share (page 15 itself says 60–70 % parasite); induced drag dominates at low speed; (6) page 10 says on a rectangular wing "lift peaks near the tips" — wrong: lift is still greatest inboard, but the tip loading is higher than the elliptical ideal, so induced drag is higher; the rectangular wing's advantage is a root-first stall; (7) page 11 says flap deployment increases wake intensity — the vortex is strongest when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean and slow (ICAO); flap redistributes lift inboard and usually weakens the tip vortex; (8) wake turbulence for the fleet: all D-0507 aircraft are wake category LIGHT; use ICAO Doc 4444 / AIP Thailand separation behind MEDIUM/HEAVY traffic (SME for current RECAT use); (9) remove the "[cite: …]" tags printed on pages 3–16.

pages.t: Understanding angle of attack and aerodynamics (lesson overview)
pages.on: Title text: angle of attack and its role in aerodynamics; propeller-aircraft image.
pages.en: Welcome to three-dimensional airflow about an aeroplane. Up to now we have often talked about airflow as if it were two-dimensional, moving smoothly over an aerofoil section. In reality an aircraft wing is finite, and that creates a truly three-dimensional flow field that changes lift, drag and stability — and even how the aircraft behind you in the circuit is affected. We begin by looking at how air flows around the whole aircraft — over the wing, fuselage and tail — and why interference between these parts matters. Then we introduce spanwise flow. Because the pressure under the wing is higher than the pressure above, the air tries to move sideways around the tip: on the lower surface it tends to flow outward toward the tip, and on the upper surface it tends to flow inward toward the root. That sideways movement sets up the signature 3D effect, the wing-tip vortices. High-pressure air from beneath the wing curls around the tip into the low-pressure region above, creating a swirling vortex that trails behind the aircraft. Those vortices create downwash, which reduces the wing's effective angle of attack and represents an energy loss that shows up as induced drag — the price of lift. We also connect this to operational reality: the trailing vortices form wake turbulence, which can persist behind an aircraft and requires spacing and awareness during take-off, landing and en-route operations. By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain why finite wings produce vortices, how downwash alters the effective angle of attack, and how design choices such as aspect ratio and winglets help manage induced drag and improve efficiency.

pages.t: Angle of attack: the cornerstone of lift
pages.on: Definition diagram (chord line, relative wind); text "AoA is the angle between the aircraft's longitudinal axis (or chord line in 2D) and the relative wind"; importance panels; "[cite: 64]" tags.
pages.en: Angle of attack, or AoA, is often called the cornerstone of lift because it is the key variable that decides how strongly the wing interacts with the airflow. AoA is the angle between the wing's chord line — or, in practical aircraft terms, a reference line aligned with the wing section — and the relative wind, which is the airflow direction opposite to the flight path. Some explanations use the aircraft's longitudinal axis, but the correct aerodynamic reference is the wing chord line, because lift is generated by the wing's orientation to the airflow. AoA matters because it largely controls the lift coefficient CL. As AoA increases, lift increases up to a limit, allowing the aircraft to fly slower, climb, or manoeuvre at a higher load factor. But AoA also controls how close you are to the stall. When the wing reaches the critical angle of attack, flow separation becomes significant: lift drops, drag rises sharply, and the wing stalls. This is why the stall is fundamentally an AoA event, not a speed event. Stall speed changes with weight, bank angle and configuration, but the critical AoA is the common trigger. Managing AoA is central to safe flight in every phase: on take-off and landing, to get the required lift at low speed; in turns, to avoid excessive AoA under higher load factors; and in turbulence, to avoid sudden AoA spikes. For engineers, AoA links directly to performance, stability and efficiency, because it shapes lift, drag and pitching-moment behaviour across the operating envelope.
pages.th: มุมปะทะ หรือ AoA มักถูกเรียกว่าหัวใจของแรงยก เพราะเป็นตัวแปรหลักที่กำหนดว่าปีกทำปฏิกิริยากับการไหลของอากาศมากแค่ไหน AoA คือมุมระหว่าง chord line ของปีก หรือในทางปฏิบัติคือเส้นอ้างอิงที่วางตามหน้าตัดปีก กับลมสัมพัทธ์ ซึ่งเป็นทิศการไหลของอากาศตรงข้ามกับทางบิน บางคำอธิบายใช้แกนตามยาวของเครื่อง แต่ค่าอ้างอิงที่ถูกต้องทางอากาศพลศาสตร์คือ chord line ของปีก เพราะแรงยกเกิดจากการวางตัวของปีกเทียบกับการไหลของอากาศ AoA สำคัญเพราะควบคุม CL เป็นหลัก เมื่อ AoA เพิ่ม แรงยกเพิ่มจนถึงขีดจำกัด ทำให้บินช้าลง ไต่ หรือเลี้ยวที่ load factor สูงขึ้นได้ แต่ AoA ก็กำหนดว่าเราใกล้ stall แค่ไหน เมื่อปีกถึงมุมปะทะวิกฤต การแยกตัวของการไหลจะมีนัยสำคัญ แรงยกลด แรงต้านเพิ่มมาก และปีก stall นี่คือเหตุผลที่ stall เป็นเหตุการณ์ของ AoA ไม่ใช่ของความเร็ว ความเร็ว stall เปลี่ยนตามน้ำหนัก มุมเอียง และ configuration แต่มุมปะทะวิกฤตคือตัวจุดชนวนร่วม การจัดการ AoA เป็นหัวใจของการบินที่ปลอดภัยในทุกช่วง ในการขึ้นและลงเพื่อให้ได้แรงยกที่ต้องการที่ความเร็วต่ำ ในการเลี้ยวเพื่อไม่ให้ AoA มากเกินภายใต้ load factor ที่สูงขึ้น และในอากาศแปรปรวนเพื่อไม่ให้ AoA พุ่งขึ้นฉับพลัน สำหรับวิศวกร AoA เชื่อมโดยตรงกับสมรรถนะ เสถียรภาพ และประสิทธิภาพ เพราะกำหนดพฤติกรรมของแรงยก แรงต้าน และโมเมนต์ก้มเงยตลอดขอบเขตการบิน

pages.t: Angle of attack vs attitude: a critical distinction
pages.on: AoA panel (relative wind vs wing), attitude panel (pitch, roll, yaw); relationship strip: constant pitch attitude with high/low airspeed; steep climb attitude vs shallow dive attitude ("HigA" label).
pages.en: This slide emphasises one safety-critical idea: the wing stalls because of angle of attack, not because of what the aeroplane looks like. Start with the left blue panel. It defines angle of attack as the angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind. Notice in the diagram and the airliner picture that the arrow labelled relative wind can point in a different direction from the aircraft's nose. That is why AoA can change even when the attitude looks almost unchanged. Now the right orange panel: attitude, the aircraft's orientation in space — pitch, roll and yaw. The small sketch makes the point that attitude is what an observer sees and what the pilot senses relative to the horizon, but attitude alone does not tell you the airflow angle at the wing. The key connection is in the green relationship section across the bottom. On the left, the aircraft holds a constant pitch attitude, but as airspeed decreases the relative wind shifts and the wing needs a higher AoA to maintain lift — high airspeed with low AoA versus low airspeed with high AoA, even though the pitch attitude looks similar. On the right you see two extremes. In a steep climb attitude AoA can be modest or high depending on the flight path; and in a shallow dive the AoA can still be high if the aircraft is descending steeply, because the relative wind comes from below. The practical takeaway is: attitude is not AoA. AoA depends on the flight path and the relative wind. That is why an aircraft can stall in a turn or a climb without looking dramatically nose-high, and can also fly safely nose-high if the AoA stays below the critical value.

pages.t: Streamline patterns: the flow around aircraft
pages.on: C172-style aircraft with streamlines; wing (accelerated flow, lower pressure); tail section ("horizontal stabilizer experiences upwash from the main wing", arrow "UPWASH FROM MAIN WING"); fuselage; garbled sentence and "[cite: 67, 70]".
pages.en: Streamline patterns show how the aircraft shapes the air around it. They help you predict where lift is produced, where drag is created and how the parts of the aircraft interact. Wing: as the airflow approaches the wing it is turned and accelerated over the upper surface. Where streamlines crowd together, the flow speed increases and static pressure drops, creating a low-pressure region above the wing. Under the wing the pressure is relatively higher, so the pressure difference across the wing generates most of the lift. Behind the wing the flow is deflected downward as downwash — evidence that the wing has changed the air's momentum. Tail section: the stabilisers sit inside the flow field created by the wing and fuselage, so their local relative wind is not the free-stream direction. The horizontal stabiliser normally sees downwash from the main wing, so the airflow reaching it is tilted downward compared with the free stream. That changes the stabiliser's effective angle of attack and directly affects trim and stability. The vertical stabiliser sees similar interactions in yaw and sideslip, which help provide directional stability and control. Fuselage: the flow along the fuselage should stay smooth, but it can be disturbed where the shape changes rapidly — around the nose, canopy, wing roots, landing-gear bays and tail junctions. These areas can create turbulence and interference drag if not designed carefully. Good aerodynamic shaping — fairings, fillets and smooth transitions — reduces separation, minimises drag and helps the wing and tail receive cleaner, more predictable airflow. Overall, streamline patterns are the big-picture tool: they show not just what each surface does, but how the wing, fuselage and tail influence one another in three-dimensional flow.

pages.t: Spanwise flow: the lateral movement of air
pages.on: 1 cause (pressure difference); 2 upper surface "air moves from wing root to tip"; 3 lower surface "air flows from tip to root"; 4 effects (tip vortex formation); C172 graphic.
pages.en: Spanwise flow is the sideways movement of air along a wing, and it happens because a real wing is finite, so pressure can leak around the tips. One, the cause: the wing creates higher pressure below and lower pressure above, and air tries to move from high pressure to low pressure. On a finite wing it can do that not only front to back but also sideways, around the tip. Two, the lower surface — root to tip: below the wing the pressure is higher than the free-stream pressure at the tip, so the air spreads outward from the root toward the tip, superimposed on the main chordwise flow. Three, the upper surface — tip to root: above the wing the low pressure is weakest at the tip, where it leaks away, so the air above the wing is drawn inward from the tip toward the root, again layered on top of the main flow. Four, the effects: at the trailing edge the outward-moving lower flow and the inward-moving upper flow meet at an angle and form a sheet of vortices that rolls up near the tip into the wing-tip vortex trailing behind the aircraft. That vortex system is energy lost to swirling airflow; it appears as induced drag and reduces the overall efficiency of the wing. This is why designers use high-aspect-ratio wings, careful twist and taper, and devices such as winglets to weaken spanwise flow and reduce vortex strength.

pages.on: Formation (high-pressure air spills over the wingtip), downwash (reduces effective AoA), energy loss (induced drag); "[cite: 80, 81]" tags.
pages.en: Tip vortices are the rotating tubes of air that trail behind a wing because a real wing has an edge where pressure can equalise. Formation: a lifting wing has higher pressure below and lower pressure above. Near the tip, high-pressure air from the underside curls around the tip toward the low-pressure region on top. That sideways spill rolls up into a swirling vortex at each wingtip, and the vortices persist behind the aircraft in the wake. Downwash: the vortex system changes the direction of the airflow behind the wing, giving it a downward component called downwash. From the wing's point of view the downwash tilts the local relative wind downward, which effectively reduces the wing's angle of attack compared with ideal two-dimensional flow. The practical result is that the wing must fly at a slightly higher geometric angle of attack to make the same lift. Energy loss — induced drag: creating vortices takes energy. The wing does work to give the air a sideways and downward motion, and that energy does not contribute to forward motion; it appears as induced drag, the price of lift. Induced drag is most significant when the wing is producing high lift — take-off, climb, slow flight and turns. This is why designers use higher-aspect-ratio wings and wing-tip devices like winglets to weaken the vortices and improve efficiency.
pages.th: tip vortex คือท่ออากาศหมุนวนที่ลากตามหลังปีก เพราะปีกจริงมีขอบที่ความดันปรับให้เท่ากันได้ การเกิด ปีกที่สร้างแรงยกมีความดันสูงด้านล่างและต่ำด้านบน ใกล้ปลายปีก อากาศความดันสูงจากด้านล่างม้วนอ้อมปลายปีกไปยังบริเวณความดันต่ำด้านบน การไหลล้นด้านข้างนี้ม้วนตัวเป็นกระแสวนที่ปลายปีกแต่ละข้าง และค้างอยู่หลังเครื่องใน wake ส่วน downwash ระบบ vortex เปลี่ยนทิศการไหลหลังปีกให้มีองค์ประกอบลง เรียกว่า downwash ในมุมมองของปีก downwash ทำให้ลมสัมพัทธ์เฉพาะที่เอียงลง ซึ่งเท่ากับลดมุมปะทะของปีกลงเมื่อเทียบกับการไหลสองมิติในอุดมคติ ผลในทางปฏิบัติคือปีกต้องบินที่มุมปะทะเชิงเรขาคณิตสูงขึ้นเล็กน้อยเพื่อให้ได้แรงยกเท่าเดิม การสูญเสียพลังงาน หรือแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำ การสร้าง vortex ต้องใช้พลังงาน ปีกทำงานเพื่อให้อากาศเคลื่อนด้านข้างและลงล่าง พลังงานนั้นไม่ได้ช่วยการเคลื่อนไปข้างหน้า แต่ปรากฏเป็นแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำ ราคาของแรงยก แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำมีมากที่สุดเมื่อปีกสร้างแรงยกสูง คือการขึ้น การไต่ การบินช้า และการเลี้ยว นี่คือเหตุผลที่ผู้ออกแบบใช้ปีก aspect ratio สูงขึ้นและอุปกรณ์ปลายปีกอย่าง winglet เพื่อลด vortex และเพิ่มประสิทธิภาพ

pages.t: Tip vortices and angle of attack: a dynamic relationship
pages.on: Four panels: low AoA (2°, weak vortex), moderate (8°), high (15°, strong vortex, F-16 vapour), near stall (18°–20°, maximum intensity before flow separation).
pages.en: Tip vortices change strength with angle of attack, because AoA largely controls how much lift the wing is producing, and lift is tied directly to the pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces. The bigger the pressure difference, the more strongly the air tries to leak around the tip and the stronger the vortex becomes. One, low angle of attack: the wing produces relatively little lift, so the pressure difference is small; with less pressure trying to equalise around the tip, spanwise flow is weaker and the tip vortices are relatively mild. Two, moderate angle of attack: lift increases and the pressure differential grows. More high-pressure air from below curls around the tip toward the low-pressure region above, so the vortex circulation increases — stronger trailing vortices and more noticeable downwash. Three, high angle of attack: the wing is producing high lift, the pressure differential is large, the spill around the tip intensifies and the vortices become strong and energetic, increasing induced drag significantly. This is why induced drag is especially prominent in slow flight, climb and high-load-factor turns. Four, near the stall: the wing is close to CLmax, so vortex strength can be near its peak while the flow is still mostly attached. Once significant separation develops, the lift distribution becomes less stable and the vortex system becomes more unsteady and less clean. In simple terms: increasing AoA increases lift, more lift increases the pressure difference, and a larger pressure difference strengthens the tip vortices — up to the edge of the stall, where separation changes the flow structure.

pages.t: Upwash and downwash: altering effective angle of attack
pages.on: Upwash ahead of the wing (increases effective AoA, "strongest near the wing root"); downwash behind (reduces effective AoA, "most pronounced near the wing tips"); impact on performance; C172 graphic.
pages.en: This picture explains an important idea: a wing does not just affect the air on the wing — it bends the airflow before the wing and after it, and that bending changes the effective angle of attack. Start with the left panel, upwash ahead of the wing. As the airflow approaches the wing it is deflected upward, so the local airflow arriving at the leading edge is tilted upward compared with the free stream. The diagram notes that upwash is often strong near the wing root, where wing–fuselage interaction is significant. Now the middle panel connects both effects to the effective AoA: the blue arrows show the air rising into the wing, and the orange arrows show what happens behind it. In the right panel, downwash behind the wing: the airflow leaves the wing deflected downward. This downwash tilts the local relative wind downward behind the wing, which reduces the effective angle of attack of anything flying in that airflow — most importantly the tailplane. That is why tail settings and trim depend on downwash: the horizontal stabiliser is not seeing the free-stream airflow but air that has already been turned by the wing. The figure also points out that downwash is closely tied to the tip vortices. Finally, the green "impact on performance" box ties it together: upwash and downwash affect lift distribution, induced drag, stability and control effectiveness. Knowing where the airflow is being turned helps explain why control surfaces are placed where they are, why tailplane incidence matters, and why induced drag is essentially the cost of creating a downwash field behind a lifting wing.

pages.on: Elliptical wing (minimum induced drag, Spitfire); rectangular wing ("lift peaks near the tips… higher induced drag", Cessna 172); tapered wing (balanced, Boeing 787).
pages.en: Spanwise lift distribution is about how the wing shares lift from root to tip, because that distribution decides how strong the tip vortices are, and therefore how much induced drag you pay for a given lift. With an elliptical wing the lift is distributed in the most aerodynamically efficient way: strongest at the root and reducing smoothly toward the tip in an elliptical pattern. That gives the weakest vortex system for the lift produced, which is why it is called the ideal distribution for minimum induced drag. The Spitfire is the famous example where designers pursued that efficiency, especially for performance at high lift when manoeuvring. A rectangular wing gives a less ideal distribution. In a simplified sense, the lift loading stays relatively high outboard compared with the ideal, which strengthens the tip vortices and increases induced drag. Its advantage is practicality: a rectangular wing is structurally simple, has predictable stall behaviour — it tends to stall at the root first — and is inexpensive to build, which is one reason it is common on training and light aircraft. A tapered wing is the compromise. By reducing chord from root to tip, the designer moves the lift distribution closer to elliptical, reducing induced drag compared with a rectangular planform, while keeping manufacture and structure more practical than a true elliptical wing. That balance is why tapered wings are widely used, from general aviation to commercial and military types. The big takeaway: a more elliptical lift distribution generally means lower induced drag, but manufacturing, structure, stall characteristics and cost decide which wing shape is the best overall choice.

pages.on: Text: formation (vortices spread outward and downward, persist several minutes); influencing factors (weight; "flap deployment increases intensity"; atmospheric conditions); operational implications (spacing).
pages.en: Wake turbulence is the hazardous by-product of lift. When a wing generates lift, it sheds trailing vortices that roll up into two counter-rotating tubes of air behind the aircraft. These vortices tend to sink and, near the ground, drift outward; in calm, stable air they can persist long enough to be a real threat to a following aircraft, especially a lighter one flying close behind on approach or departure. The strength of wake turbulence depends mainly on how much lift the aircraft is producing. In practice that means heavier aircraft generate stronger vortices, and vortex strength also increases when the aircraft is slow and at a high angle of attack — take-off, initial climb, approach and landing. Configuration matters too: the vortex is strongest when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean and slow; flaps change the lift distribution and usually weaken the tip vortex, but the dominant driver is still the lift requirement set by weight, speed and angle of attack. Atmospheric conditions decide how quickly the wake dissipates: a crosswind can move it sideways, stable air lets it stay organised longer, and turbulence and mixing break it up faster. Operationally, this is why controllers and procedures enforce spacing behind larger aircraft, and why pilots avoid flying directly below and behind another aircraft's flight path. On take-off, a common technique is to rotate before the preceding aircraft's rotation point, climb above its path and stay upwind of its track if there is a crosswind. On landing, the aim is to stay above the preceding aircraft's glide path and touch down beyond its touchdown point when appropriate. Understanding where the vortices go and when they are strongest is essential for safe separation and for preventing an unexpected roll upset close to the ground.

pages.t: Induced drag: the price of lift
pages.on: Four panels: definition, mechanism (downwash tilts lift vector rearward), component (rearward force; "a significant part of total drag at cruising speeds"), efficiency impact (pie chart: induced drag "major contributor" in typical cruise).
pages.en: Induced drag is often called the price of lift because it exists only when the wing is producing lift. One, definition: induced drag is the part of drag that appears as a direct consequence of generating lift with a finite wing. Two, mechanism: a lifting wing creates downwash behind it. That downwash tilts the local relative wind downward, which means the aerodynamic force produced by the wing is no longer perpendicular to the free stream; the resultant is tilted slightly rearward. Three, component: when that tilted force is resolved into components, there is a rearward component that opposes forward motion — that rearward component is induced drag. Four, efficiency impact: induced drag is most significant when the aircraft needs high lift — take-off, climb, slow flight and turning — and it can be the major part of total drag at low speeds. Designers reduce it with higher-aspect-ratio wings, a better spanwise lift distribution, and devices like winglets that weaken the tip vortices and the downwash.
pages.th: แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำมักถูกเรียกว่าราคาของแรงยก เพราะมีอยู่เฉพาะเมื่อปีกสร้างแรงยก ข้อหนึ่ง นิยาม แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำคือส่วนของแรงต้านที่เกิดเป็นผลโดยตรงจากการสร้างแรงยกด้วยปีกที่มีความยาวจำกัด ข้อสอง กลไก ปีกที่สร้างแรงยกทำให้เกิด downwash หลังปีก downwash ทำให้ลมสัมพัทธ์เฉพาะที่เอียงลง แรงทางอากาศพลศาสตร์ของปีกจึงไม่ตั้งฉากกับกระแสอิสระอีกต่อไป แรงลัพธ์เอียงไปข้างหลังเล็กน้อย ข้อสาม องค์ประกอบ เมื่อแยกแรงที่เอียงนั้นเป็นองค์ประกอบ จะได้องค์ประกอบไปข้างหลังที่ต้านการเคลื่อนที่ไปข้างหน้า องค์ประกอบนี้คือแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำ ข้อสี่ ผลต่อประสิทธิภาพ แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำมีมากที่สุดเมื่อเครื่องต้องการแรงยกสูง คือการขึ้น การไต่ การบินช้า และการเลี้ยว และอาจเป็นส่วนใหญ่ของแรงต้านรวมที่ความเร็วต่ำ ผู้ออกแบบลดแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำด้วยปีก aspect ratio สูงขึ้น การกระจายแรงยกตามแนวปีกที่ดีขึ้น และอุปกรณ์อย่าง winglet ที่ทำให้ tip vortex และ downwash อ่อนลง

pages.t: Induced drag coefficient: quantifying the effect
pages.on: CDi = k·CL²; k-factor (aspect ratio, planform); graph CDi vs CL (parabolic, 0–0.04); high CL (climb) vs low CL (cruise); application.
pages.en: The induced drag coefficient puts a number on the price of lift and shows how quickly it grows as lift demand increases. The formula is CDi = k × CL². It says that the induced drag coefficient rises with the square of the lift coefficient. What does the k-factor mean? The constant k captures how efficiently the wing produces lift with minimal vortex losses: a lower k means a more efficient wing and less induced drag for the same CL. In practice k depends mainly on aspect ratio and on how close the lift distribution is to the ideal. A common way to write it is k = 1 ÷ (π × e × AR), where AR is the aspect ratio and e is the Oswald efficiency factor — how close to elliptical the lift distribution is. A higher AR and a higher e both reduce k and improve efficiency. Why CL squared matters: because the relationship is squared, induced drag grows very quickly when lift demand rises. That is why induced drag becomes dominant in slow flight, climb and turns — a higher load factor means a higher CL — and why you feel a big performance penalty when flying slowly and pulling for lift. Application: this equation is used in performance prediction and optimisation. It helps build the drag polar, estimate power and thrust required, compare wing designs, and understand how winglets, higher aspect ratio or a better planform reduce induced drag and improve climb, cruise efficiency and glide performance.
pages.th: สัมประสิทธิ์แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำทำให้ราคาของแรงยกเป็นตัวเลข และแสดงว่ามันเพิ่มเร็วแค่ไหนเมื่อต้องการแรงยกมากขึ้น สูตรคือ CDi = k × CL² หมายความว่าสัมประสิทธิ์แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำเพิ่มตามกำลังสองของสัมประสิทธิ์แรงยก ค่า k หมายถึงอะไร ค่าคงที่ k แสดงว่าปีกสร้างแรงยกได้มีประสิทธิภาพแค่ไหนโดยสูญเสียกับ vortex น้อยที่สุด k ต่ำหมายถึงปีกมีประสิทธิภาพกว่าและแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำน้อยกว่าที่ CL เดียวกัน ในทางปฏิบัติ k ขึ้นกับ aspect ratio และความใกล้เคียงอุดมคติของการกระจายแรงยกเป็นหลัก เขียนได้ทั่วไปว่า k = 1 ÷ (π × e × AR) โดย AR คือ aspect ratio และ e คือ Oswald efficiency factor ซึ่งบอกว่าการกระจายแรงยกใกล้วงรีแค่ไหน AR สูงขึ้นและ e สูงขึ้นทำให้ k ลดลงและประสิทธิภาพดีขึ้น ทำไม CL ยกกำลังสองจึงสำคัญ เพราะความสัมพันธ์เป็นกำลังสอง แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำจึงเพิ่มเร็วมากเมื่อความต้องการแรงยกเพิ่ม นี่คือเหตุผลที่แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำเด่นในการบินช้า การไต่ และการเลี้ยว (load factor สูงหมายถึง CL สูง) และทำไมจึงรู้สึกถึงการเสียสมรรถนะมากเมื่อบินช้าและดึงเพื่อเอาแรงยก การใช้งาน สมการนี้ใช้ทำนายและปรับสมรรถนะให้เหมาะสม ช่วยสร้าง drag polar ประมาณกำลังและแรงขับที่ต้องใช้ เปรียบเทียบการออกแบบปีก และเข้าใจว่า winglet, aspect ratio ที่สูงขึ้น หรือ planform ที่ดีขึ้นลดแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำและปรับปรุงการไต่ ประสิทธิภาพ cruise และการร่อนได้อย่างไร

pages.on: Three panels: increase aspect ratio (sailplane); winglets and tip tanks (airliner with blended winglets); wing twist (washout) and camber variation.
pages.en: To minimise induced drag you are essentially trying to weaken the wing-tip vortex system by improving how lift is produced across the span and how the tip flow behaves. Increase aspect ratio: a longer span relative to chord reduces the intensity of the tip vortices and lowers the downwash for the same lift. That directly reduces induced drag and improves efficiency in climb and cruise, and especially at low speeds. The trade-offs are higher structural bending loads, extra weight and sometimes a slower roll response, so designers balance span against strength, cost and handling. Use winglets or tip devices: winglets, raked tips and some tip-tank designs act like end plates or vortex-management devices. They reduce the leakage of high-pressure air around the tip and reshape the vortex system so less energy is lost to swirling airflow. The benefit is better fuel efficiency and range, but they add weight and structural loads at the tip and must be carefully optimised so that their own drag does not cancel the gain. Optimise wing twist and camber toward the tips: induced drag is minimised when the spanwise lift distribution is close to ideal and the tip is not overworked. Designers use washout — geometric twist, aerodynamic twist (changing the aerofoil camber along the span), or both — to shift lift inboard and manage tip loading. This improves efficiency and also improves stall behaviour, because the root stalls before the tip, preserving aileron effectiveness near the stall. In short, reduce induced drag with more span, smarter tips and a better lift distribution, balanced against the structural and handling penalties that come with them.
pages.th: การลดแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำโดยพื้นฐานคือการทำให้ระบบ wing-tip vortex อ่อนลง ด้วยการปรับวิธีสร้างแรงยกตลอดแนวปีกและพฤติกรรมการไหลที่ปลายปีก เพิ่ม aspect ratio ปีกที่ยาวขึ้นเทียบกับ chord ลดความแรงของ tip vortex และลด downwash ที่แรงยกเท่าเดิม ลดแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำโดยตรง และเพิ่มประสิทธิภาพในการไต่และ cruise โดยเฉพาะที่ความเร็วต่ำ ข้อแลกเปลี่ยนคือภาระดัดของโครงสร้างสูงขึ้น น้ำหนักเพิ่ม และบางครั้ง roll ตอบสนองช้าลง ผู้ออกแบบจึงต้องชั่งความยาวปีกกับความแข็งแรง ต้นทุน และการบังคับ ใช้ winglet หรืออุปกรณ์ปลายปีก winglet, raked tip และ tip tank บางแบบทำหน้าที่เหมือนแผ่นปิดปลาย (end plate) หรืออุปกรณ์จัดการ vortex ลดการรั่วของอากาศความดันสูงอ้อมปลายปีก และปรับรูประบบ vortex ให้เสียพลังงานกับอากาศหมุนวนน้อยลง ข้อดีคือประหยัดเชื้อเพลิงและพิสัยไกลขึ้น แต่เพิ่มน้ำหนักและภาระโครงสร้างที่ปลายปีก และต้องออกแบบอย่างพิถีพิถันไม่ให้แรงต้านของตัวมันเองหักล้างประโยชน์ ปรับการบิดปีกและ camber ไปทางปลาย แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำต่ำสุดเมื่อการกระจายแรงยกตามแนวปีกใกล้อุดมคติและปลายปีกไม่ได้ทำงานหนักเกินไป ผู้ออกแบบใช้ washout ทั้งการบิดเชิงเรขาคณิต การบิดเชิงอากาศพลศาสตร์ (เปลี่ยน camber ของ aerofoil ตามแนวปีก) หรือทั้งสองอย่าง เพื่อย้ายแรงยกเข้าด้านในและจัดการภาระที่ปลายปีก ช่วยทั้งประสิทธิภาพและพฤติกรรม stall เพราะโคนปีก stall ก่อนปลาย ทำให้ aileron ยังใช้ได้ใกล้ stall สรุปคือ ลดแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำด้วยปีกที่ยาวขึ้น ปลายปีกที่ฉลาดขึ้น และการกระจายแรงยกที่ดีขึ้น โดยชั่งกับข้อเสียด้านโครงสร้างและการบังคับที่ตามมา

pages.t: Induced drag vs total drag in cruise flight
pages.on: 30–40 % induced drag in cruise (airliner); 60–70 % parasite (fighter); graph drag components vs airspeed with "cruise flight region"; speed relationship Di ∝ 1/V² ("doubling the speed reduces induced drag by a factor of four").
pages.en: These cruise percentages are a reasonable rule of thumb, but they are not fixed. The split between induced and parasite drag depends mainly on how much lift the wing must produce — weight and load factor — and how fast you are flying, plus configuration, altitude and Mach effects. Why parasite drag dominates in cruise: in cruise the aircraft flies at a relatively high speed and a relatively low lift coefficient compared with take-off and slow flight. That keeps induced drag smaller, while parasite drag — skin friction plus form drag plus interference drag — becomes the larger share and grows with speed. Why induced drag falls with speed — the 1/V² idea: in steady level flight L ≈ W, so CL = 2W ÷ (ρV²S). As V increases, the required CL decreases with 1/V². The induced drag coefficient follows CDi = k·CL². Combine the two and, for the same weight and configuration at a given density, the induced drag force ends up decreasing roughly with 1/V². That is why induced drag is a big deal at low speed and much less dominant at cruise speed. What about the 30–40 % versus 60–70 % split? Many aircraft in cruise do see parasite drag as the majority and induced drag as the smaller portion, but the exact split swings with weight (heavier → more induced), altitude and density, Mach and compressibility, and wing efficiency — aspect ratio, winglets and so on. Near the best-L/D speed the induced and parasite components are about equal; at higher cruise speeds parasite drag takes over more.

pages.t: CL–α and CL–CD relationships: performance insights
pages.on: CL–α graph: high aspect ratio (sailplane, steeper slope, stalls at lower α) vs low aspect ratio (fighter); CL–CD polar with minimum drag, best L/D, maximum lift; application panel.
pages.en: The CL–alpha graph — what it tells you. The CL–alpha curve shows how the lift coefficient changes as the angle of attack increases. Slope — the lift-curve slope: the steeper the slope, the more lift you gain per degree of AoA. For a finite wing the slope is reduced by downwash, and higher-aspect-ratio wings have a steeper slope because they generate less downwash for the same lift. A common engineering form is a = a0 ÷ (1 + a0 ÷ (π·e·AR)), where a is the 3D wing slope, a0 is the 2D aerofoil slope, e is the efficiency factor and AR the aspect ratio. Zero-lift angle: where the curve crosses CL = 0; it shifts with camber. CLmax and stall: the peak, or where the curve stops being linear, marks CLmax and the onset of the stall — directly tied to low-speed limits and stall margin. Performance insight: CL–alpha tells you how sensitive the wing is to AoA, where the stall occurs, and how configuration changes — flaps, slats — shift the curve. The CL–CD polar — what it tells you: it shows the drag cost of producing lift. Minimum drag point, CDmin: the lowest-drag point on the curve — but that is not maximum efficiency. Best efficiency, maximum L/D: on the polar, the best L/D, CL ÷ CD, occurs where a line from the origin is tangent to the curve. Induced drag effect: as CL rises, CD rises faster, roughly parabolically, because induced drag grows with lift demand. Performance insight: the polar tells you the best-glide, best-efficiency operating region, and how expensive high lift is in drag terms. (The recording stops here.)
